newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE - Life out of balance, Amerindians meet to save Earth.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Life out of balance, Amerindians meet to save Earth.

text.p: Believing the modern world is spinning dangerously out of balance, native Indian leaders from around the Western Hemisphere are preparing to break 500 years of virtual silence in a bid to rescue Mother Earth.

A rainbow confederation of more than 400 elders and shamen will hold council in a traditional ceremonial long-house or "maloca" in a remote village deep in the Colombian Amazon region for 10 days starting on June 19.

"Life is out of balance because man became disconnected from the basic essence of the cosmos," event organiser Francisco Quiroga told Reuters. "The main objective of the meeting is for peace. But there cannot be real peace until there's peace between man and Mother Earth."

Quiroga, born and bred in Bogota, Colombia's capital, describes himself as mixed-race with a strong attachment to the "sacred ways of his indigenous ancestors." Indian leaders see him as an important envoy, capable of bridging the gap between their traditions and the white man's world.

Through the Sendama Foundation, an organisation he heads in Bogota, Quiroga has helped raised more than $300,000 to bring together scores of groups from every corner of the hemisphere, including U.S.-based Hopi and Apaches, Canadian Inuits, Brazilian Kayapos and Colombian Kogis, in the village of Araracuara in Colombia's southeast Amazonas province.

The village is linked to the outside world only by a labyrinth of rivers or a single weekly flight to the capital, often fully booked months in advance. But for this meeting Colombia's air force has agreed to airlift the indigenous elders from Bogota to the jungle aboard on two giant Hercules transport planes.

Quiroga said the delegates would issue a communique at the end of their so-called Reunion of the Indigenous Elders and Priests of the Americas but that outsiders would not be allowed to witness meetings and religious ceremonies. The precise agenda has not been disclosed but Quiroga said the tribal elders would concentrate on core issues of how ancient prophecies and teachings can be used to solve current problems affecting all humankind.

"The planet has been devastated. The elders consider the time of passive resistance has passed. Now is the time to take action to save Mother Earth. The prophecies say that the time for a new dawn has come," he said.

"The elders have not spoken out like for the last 500 years. I don't know how they will pass out their message. But if through his arrogance the white man does not understand he will have to suffer the consequences."
Quiroga said "peripheral" topics such as land rights, racial discrimination and the preservation of language and culture would not form a central part of the meeting.

"Indigenous people end up being drawn into Western schemes of politics and become highly politicized when they campaign for specific rights. We want to ... avoid falling into a political trap," he said.

Elders who attended a smaller meeting in Guatemala in 1995 chose to stage this month's meeting in Colombia based on a prophecy of the Arizona-based Hopi, which says: "The people of the centre must unite the eagle of the north with the condor of the south."

Though perhaps not the geographical centre of the Americas, Quiroga argued Colombia was a centre of spiritual energy where the Andes mountains and Amazon jungle came together on the route between North and South America.

Once the elders' work is done the fate of the world will hinge on whether their "errant brother," the white man, sets aside pride and arrogance -- the attitudes that led him to invade the Americas more than 500 years ago.

"Man has cancer of the mind, which results in the uncontrollable production of technology and material things. The call is for man to get back in balance with the heart of the sky and the heart of Mother Earth and begin to dance the cosmic dance again," Quiroga said.
